beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sai Pranavi J. This video is about a small fix to our regulatory intelligence pipeline, teaching it to ask a local AI model for help on headlines it couldn't classify, and why the honest result was a model that correctly said I don't know most of the time.
beats.new_visual_element: Personal-intro card: fellow's name + one-line summary of what the video covers, spoken

shot.note: Same pattern as this fellow's other episodes' B01.

beats.narration_text: Twenty-one real headlines were falling through our classifier to Unknown Source. Over the last few weeks, keyword fixes brought that down to eight. This week: what happens when you hand those eight to an AI model instead of another keyword rule.
beats.new_visual_element: A counter ticking 21 to 13 resolved to 8 remaining, landing on 8

beats.narration_text: Before touching any code, I re-ran the actual classifier, the real function, not a copy, against all 21 database rows. Thirteen are already resolved by fixes already shipped. The remaining eight are headlines like Understanding the Regulations of 24-Hour Trading, or Know Your Client: Key Requirements for Financial Services. Generic enough that no fixed keyword list can catch them without also catching things that have nothing to do with financial regulation.
beats.new_visual_element: 2-3 real example headlines shown directly, with a caption 'no keyword list resolves these safely'

shot.note: [Source: B2-VERIFICATION.md 2026-10-06 addendum] Real verbatim DB titles, not paraphrased.

beats.narration_text: So instead of one more brittle keyword rule, I added a new step: for exactly the items still marked Unknown Source, and only those, ask a local AI model to pick the best-fitting category from the four we already track, or say none of them fit. Every other item is never touched. If the model's answer isn't one of the four real categories, or the call fails for any reason, the item keeps its original label. Nothing gets silently mislabeled.
beats.new_visual_element: Pipeline diagram: the new node inserted between the existing classifier and the next step, with a highlighted 'only acts on Unknown Source' condition

shot.note: [Source: workflow.dev.json, Layer 2 - LLM Source Classification node] Diagram must show the conditional gate, not just narrate it.

beats.narration_text: I tested this against the real eight headlines, running the exact code that would ship, not a simulation. Zero of the thirteen already-resolved items were touched. Of the eight, the model correctly classified one, an enforcement-actions piece that does belong to one of our tracked categories. It declined to guess on the other seven. I also killed the connection to the AI model entirely and reran it: every item kept its original label, nothing broke.
beats.new_visual_element: The 4 real numbers on screen together: 0 mutated, 1 resolved, 7 declined, 0 errors, plus the one resolved headline and its new label

shot.note: [Source: B2-VERIFICATION.md live-verification section] All 4 numbers must be visible together.

beats.narration_text: One out of eight is not a big number, and I'm not going to pretend it is. But it's the correct number. Those seven declined headlines are genuinely generic: a KYC explainer, a 24-hour-trading explainer, law-firm monthly digests. They don't actually belong to any of the four categories this pipeline tracks. A model that forced a label onto all eight would have looked more impressive and been more wrong.
beats.new_visual_element: Statement card: '1 of 8, and that's the correct number', with the 7 declined headlines dimmed below it

shot.note: No softening — frame 1-of-8 as correct, not as a shortfall, per house style.

beats.narration_text: When you add an AI model to a pipeline, the win isn't always a bigger number. Sometimes the win is a system that knows the difference between I can classify this and I shouldn't guess, and does the second one on purpose.
